rv.q: Diana is a rollicking journey that's made even better by the addition of a cocktail…Or three.
It’s so campy you circle the date on your calendar in glitter pen.
It’s just a regular, run-of-the-mill mess, a well-intended celebration of a beloved figure undone by one bad turn after another.
The musical's treatment of Diana's story feels superficial and often tone-deaf, reducing a complex and tragic figure to a series of musical theater clichés.
This sameness proves, over time, to be difficult to bear.
What makes “Diana” so perverse is its refiguring of a real-life tragedy — with survivors who remain in the public eye — into a sort of limp and misshapen rom-com.
It’s just exploitative, doing to the Princess of Wales pretty much what the tabloid press — let alone the monarchy — did to her in the first place.

But the almost impressively artless new Broadway musical from "Memphis" creators Joe DiPietro and David Bryan — which does plenty of its own speculation about the dead — lacks any similar claim to daring, originality or taste.
But everything and everyone this musical touches is somehow vulgarized.
This was among the most terrible ideas in the long history of Broadway.
This number, titled "The Dress," encapsulates the combination of bad taste and tasty badness that is Diana, one of the most enjoyable Broadway farragos of the 21st century so far.

Devoid of insight and ricocheting between dull vulgarity and vacuous hero worship, the show, which had its official opening Wednesday at the Longacre Theatre, is less edifying than a scroll through the archives of the tabloids.
And, well, it is the most fun I’ve had in a theatre in a long, long time.
For all of her strengths, though, I don’t think DeWaal has the “It Factor” the role really needs; there seems to be little chance DeWaal will become our next Patti LuPone.
Why this musical exists and why anyone would want to go see it remains a mystery.
And what the hell is it supposed to be?
But it’s hard to see how “Diana The Musical” is so much less so.
But this musical makes it difficult to do that.
Contrary to the vicious ridicule it was greeted with on social media, “Diana” is not a disaster – it’s just not very good.

In truth, Diana isn’t much more insipid than any number of musical hagiographies that have popped up in recent decades, and director Christopher Ashley, to his credit, guides it with a light hand, having fun with the dishier aspects of the story rather than wallowing in the pathos.
It is bloodless, procedural, and, in Christopher Ashley’s staging, constantly, exhaustingly turned up to 11.
Puerile, tasteless, and simplistic, this tabloid tuner is the first show to be streamed on TV before it opens on Broadway and will probably suffer big time at the box office as a result.
Diana is a musical that feels fundamentally uncomfortable with its own subject matter.

It is a terrific feminist, anti-royalist story (book by Joe DiPietro) of what happens when a woman, facing a powerful institution (the “Royal Family”), has the gumption to stand up and fight for her dignity.
The musical feels less like a thoughtful examination of Diana's life and more like a greatest hits compilation, hitting the major beats without much depth or nuance.
Diana is a rock/pop musical that fast-forwards through seventeen years of the princess’s life in such a ludicrous manner you’d be forgiven for calling it a farce.
More than any other word, I would describe it as dull.

tn.cat: Best Costume Design of a Musical

cn.t: Critics savage Diana as superficial, tasteless, and artless, with most finding it neither bad enough to be campy fun nor good enough to be genuinely entertaining, though a few embrace its campy spectacle.

sg.ra: Longacre's proscenium is narrow (35ft wide, 34'10" high) and the house is shallow, so Row D sits very close without neck-craning; Center Orchestra rows D-L fall inside the mezzanine overhang line (which starts around Row H) but the overhang is shallow enough that top-of-stage cut-off is not reported here, unlike deeper houses.

Longacre is a small-to-mid house (1,077 seats) so 'rear' orchestra is still close by Broadway standards; rows L-N sit behind the mezzanine overhang line (starts ~H) which trims a small slice of upper stage but preserves intimacy and drops the price noticeably versus premium D-K.

Longacre's mezzanine is 'not too high' per SeatPlan - the overhang from the balcony only starts at Row B, so Row A gets a clean head-on elevated view, and unusually generous front-row legroom is a Longacre-specific quirk called out on BroadwayWorld.

Rows D-E sit under the balcony overhang (starts Row B) but Longacre's balcony is small (249 seats, 7 rows) so the overhang depth is modest; sources consistently flag D-E as the honest middle-ground for elevated sightlines before rows F-J start feeling far from the stage.

Longacre's mezzanine rake flattens toward the back per SeatPlan ('the rake may also be slightly too shallow if a taller patron is sitting in front'), and rows F-J are explicitly called out as 'problematic' and 'not the best on account of their considerable distance from the stage' - the small house becomes a disadvantage here since the balcony takes over the better upper-level views.

Longacre-specific quirk: the front balcony rail sits high enough that multiple TripAdvisor reviewers at 5'5" and 5'7" had to lean over the bar the whole show (Macbeth 2022, Swept Away-era 2025), so Row B beats Row A for most patrons - the opposite of the usual 'front row is always best' advice. Also avoid the four structural pillars between rows B and C on the center aisles.

sg.vl: Skip for any show with detail
sg.ra: Longacre's balcony is the oldest-school part of the house - a 1913 Henry B. Herts design with four structural pillars between B-C and a steep rake that gets sound-dead at the back; SeatPlan explicitly warns 'sound quality may be inferior toward the rear' and rows D-G compound distance + pillar risk + tight legroom.
